answer:
PostHog's communication tier list ranks public, written, asynchronous channels highest and interruptive ones lowest. Some entries on it are jokes.

- Best (S tier): pull requests. [1]
- A tier: requests for comments and GitHub issues. [1]
- B tier: public Slack channels. [1]
- Worse: private messages are D tier, email is E tier, and carrier pigeon, chemtrails and fax machine are joke entries in C and D. [1]
- Worst (F tier): tapping someone on the shoulder and saying "You got a minute?". [1]

The rest of the handbook is consistent with this ranking:

- Slack is for informal communication, and you should chat publicly by default. [2]
- Too much context in a private place can hurt contributors who don't have Slack access. [3]
- Email is described as one of the worst ways to reach the ICP, the customers PostHog targets. [4]

answer:
Engineering hiring has four stages:
1. Culture screen: the Talent team runs a 20-30 min call. They make an initial assessment of fit for the job, culture and communication style, and they sort out logistics [1].
2. Technical screen: an hour-long interview with one of our engineers. It can be architecture design or a deeper dive into past technical experience, with no whiteboarding or brain teasers [2].
3. Culture & motivation chat: a short 15 min chat with Tim or James, who are co-founders or execs [3].
4. SuperDay: this is the final stage. It is a paid full day of work, and the decision is based on the day's output [4].

The handbook's "stage 3 & stage 4" wording fits the numbering above, but it doesn't list the stages as a numbered sequence. I ordered them by the page flow [5]. For full-stack roles, the SuperDay task is to build a small web service [4]. A separate SuperDay prep guide says the day also includes a debugging session, a check-in call and a short chat with a co-founder or exec [6].

PostHog uses a context-based expense policy. You're trusted to decide, with transparency and accountability.

- **Test before spending:** Ask whether you can clearly explain why the expense is in PostHog's best interest. Also ask whether you'd be comfortable explaining it publicly to the whole team [1]. If you're in doubt, ask your team lead for context, not permission [2].
- **Limit:** Each person gets a single User Limit of $5,000 per month in Brex. It covers individual subscriptions, coworking, equipment, training and similar. Laptops and Mac Studio Monitors are the exception, so ping #team-people-and-ops for those [3]. If you need a higher limit, request it on Brex [3].
- **Transparency:** All expenses are visible company-wide [4]. Team leads get monthly reports on their direct reports' spending [5].
- **Receipts:** Expenses over $75 or £75 need itemized receipts attached and the memo updated within 14 days [6]. A good memo covers what, why and context [7].
- **UK staff:** Use your Revolut if the expense is over £75 and has UK VAT on it. Otherwise use your Brex [8].
- **Offsites:** If you're joining an offsite, use only the offsite budget, not your User Limit [9].
- **Review:** Finance reviews all Brex expenses over $1000, a random sample of those under $1000, and all Revolut expenses [10].
- **Why it matters:** If people consistently skip receipts and memos, the company may need rigid pre-approvals. It may also treat repeated violations as performance management issues [11].
- **New tools:** Adopting a new company-wide tool or vendor has its own process [12].

answer:
Mostly yes on management, with a caveat. You decide what the team works on, but you shouldn't set tasks for people.

**Manager?** By default a team lead also manages the people on their team. Occasionally they don't, for example when a new small team has just been created [1]. The handbook also says team leads don't necessarily equal managers [2]. Management is light. Managers must not set tasks for their direct reports, because that isn't how small teams work [3].

**Who decides what to build?** You do. The team lead has the final say in the team's decision-making, including what to build [4]. Even so, the handbook says managers shouldn't set tasks for people in small teams [4].

**Extra jobs as lead:**
- Make sure the team's regular work happens: quarterly goals, a prioritized roadmap, talking to customers, monitoring metrics, fixing bugs and so on. Enable the team to do it rather than doing it all yourself [2].
- When you take over, run /org-change in Slack. It creates a tracked issue with the right checklist [2].
- Set up support processes: Slack channels, Zendesk integration, a fair support rotation, and SLA and support hero notifications [2].
- Keep Marketing and Billing informed about product progress [5]. Give at least 2-3 weeks' notice of a product launch [5].
- Organize and lead quarterly goal setting, and document the goals on your team page [6].
- Make sure the team's sprint takes place regularly [7].

answer:
Sign commits with Secretive (slightly preferred) or 1Password. Signing proves you authored a commit, because the Author field can be forged [1][2].

**Secretive:**
1. Create a new key in Secretive. Name it "Git signing key" and set Protection Level to Notify [3].
2. In Secretive > Integrations, click Git Signing and pick that key. Then paste the ~/.gitconfig and ~/.gitallowedsigners snippets into those files, merging into your existing ~/.gitconfig if you have one [3].
3. Set SSH_AUTH_SOCK for your shell as Secretive instructs [3].
4. Copy your public key. Add it in your GitHub SSH keys settings with key type Signing Key [3].
5. Test with an empty commit on a new branch and push it. You should see a green Verified badge [4].

**1Password:** follow the 1Password git commit signing guide [5].

**After setup:** turn on "Flag unsigned commits as unverified" in your GitHub profile [6].

**Troubleshooting:** if Touch ID prompts you on every commit, your key has Protection Level Require Authentication. Generate a new key with Notify [7].

Push the branch to GitHub — you should see a green Verified badge on the commit.

answer:
Usually yes, but only by deleting person profiles, not by editing the data. Events and properties can't be amended once they're in Clickhouse [1]. The steps and caveats are:

1. The customer should first stop sending the sensitive data, either by redacting it client-side or by setting up a CDP transformation. If they don't, it will keep arriving after deletion [2].
2. Delete the person profile associated with the events that hold the sensitive data. This can be done in the app or via the API. The profile is removed immediately, but the events can take days or even weeks to go [1].
3. If they aren't using person profiles, this method isn't available. They would have to delete the entire project that contains the sensitive data [3].
4. For customers spending $20K or more a year, the Clickhouse team may be able to write a targeted deletion or property amendment query. There are no guarantees, and it takes a lot of time [4]. To request it, escalate a support ticket with the event and property names. It helps to get a SQL query from the customer that identifies the data, and to check that its results match what they expect. Set the expectation that this can also take days or weeks [4].
5. If they need the data gone immediately, the only option is to delete the project [5].

answer:
**Closing it:** Once you've identified the root cause, implemented a fix, and confirmed customer-facing services are back to normal, type /inc close in the incident channel [1]. Also mark the incident as resolved on the status page [1].

**Post-mortem for a major incident:** it needs a team call, and the steps are:
1. Fill out the template in the incident page. You'll be prompted to do this when the incident is resolved [2].
2. Fill out the Summary and DERP sections in detail, because these are the most valuable [2].
3. Check that the timeline is accurate [2].
4. Schedule the call and invite engineering@posthog.com and any key stakeholders [2].
5. Review as a group, and update the post-mortem as you go to capture new details and ideas [2].
6. Share the outcomes. The final summary gets posted in #incidents, and this should happen automatically when you mark the post-mortem as complete [2].

After closing, step away and clear your head. Bring someone else up to speed and hand off any outstanding customer communications [3].

Some incidents also need a public post-mortem. That applies if the incident caused permanent data impact, directly disrupted customers' own services, or caused extended unavailability [4]. A public post-mortem goes through internal review before it's published [4].

**What a beta needs**
- It should give users value and have base functionality. It doesn't need to be feature complete, but it should be more than a mocked-up front end [1].
- It should have a title, a description, a feedback button, a payload with `product_key`, and a link to basic docs [2]. Mark the docs as beta [3].
- It should have a feature owner [3].
- Betas don't need to be performant for high-volume users and can have big bugs. These should be clearly marked in the UI [4].
- Product teams write the documentation [5].
- Use the early access feature flag with a `product_key` in the payload so people get the product in their sidebar [6].

**Marketing heads-up for the full launch**
- Marketing and billing teams typically ask for at least two weeks' notice before a major launch [7].
- The team lead should give 2-3 weeks' notice [8].
- If you plan to launch in a specific quarter, you MUST tell Marketing at the start of that quarter [9].

It also helps to tell Marketing when the beta goes live, so they can add it to the changelog and plan announcements [10].

answer:
**Who maintains the SDKs:** A small dedicated SDK team (@PostHog/team-client-libraries) helps drive direction and coordination, but maintenance is shared across engineering [1]. Engineers across teams do the work if they volunteer for the SDK support rotation, contribute when their product needs SDK changes, or pick up SDK work during hack days or spare capacity [2].

**What to do on SDK support duty:** Each week one team member is the SDK Support Hero, and your main job is making sure SDK questions get attention across all SDKs, including mobile [3]. Specifically:
- Watch escalated SDK tickets in Zendesk and new issues in the SDK repos, such as posthog-js, posthog-python, posthog-ios, posthog-android and posthog-flutter [3].
- Route issues to the relevant team. Assign the Zendesk ticket to that team and use the team's label in GitHub. If no team fits a GitHub issue, label it SDK Support Hero [4].
- Then work on SDK Zendesk tickets and GitHub issues labelled SDK Support Hero (or unlabelled, which you should label). Use your judgement on effort, reward, urgency and your skill set [5].
- Prioritise mobile issues for faster turnaround, because fixes can take weeks or months to roll out. Validate carefully and avoid breaking changes, since mistakes are hard to correct after release [6].
- At the end of the week, write a public handover message in #support-client-libraries covering work in progress, how the rotation is going, and any learnings or feedback [7].

answer: Your first three months of commission are paid at 100% fixed OTE, based on your start date [1]. Because July 21st is after the 15th, the rule for starting on or after the 15th applies. The handbook's example is a Jan 17th start: two months of 100% fixed OTE in the start quarter, plus one month of 100% fixed OTE in the next quarter, and two months of quota'ed commission [1]. Applied to July 21st, that means Q3 has two months at 100% fixed OTE and Q4 has one month at 100% fixed OTE. The other two Q4 months are on your attainment. The handbook's timeline for a 7/21/2025 hire shows this: Q3 is 1 month not employed and 2 months at 100% fixed OTE, and Q4 is 1 month at 100% fixed OTE and 2 months at 'your attainment' OTE [2]. After that, commission follows your role's normal plan. For TAEs, payments are made at the end of January, April, July and October [3].

- They must share a copy of their current contract, pricing or bank statement as proof [2].
- They must sign an annual PostHog contract worth $20k+/year, paid up front. It starts when their current contract expires [2].
- Overlap usage must be proportionate to the new contract. For example, a $50k contract with 6 months left gets $25k of free credit [3].
- The competitor has to be 'real'. As a general rule, anyone we've written a comparison article about counts [4].
- We have final discretion on who gets the deal [5].
- We can still offer a standard 2-4 week free trial before they sign [6].
- Normal commission rules apply. Commission is paid in the quarter in which the customer pays their invoice [7].

answer:
Refunds are handled in four steps: check the scenario and eligibility, work out the amount, decide between a credit and a refund, then issue it.

**1. Scenarios and eligibility.** We refund or credit for four scenarios: learning curve, unexpected stardom, under attack and wrong setup. The customer must also meet these criteria:
- The request is made within 30 days of the billing date [1].
- The customer gives a reasonable explanation that fits one of the scenarios [2].
- The account shows no signs of fraud or abuse [3].

**2. Repeat incidents.** The first incident follows the standard policy, and we give guidance on preventing a repeat [4]. If a later incident happens and the customer hasn't fixed the issue, offer a partial refund of up to 50% while they fix it [5]. For a third incident or beyond, refunds may be declined unless there are extraordinary circumstances [6].

**3. Channels.** Requests can arrive as an in-app ticket, which Support reviews and answers [7]. For large accounts managed by an AE, the AE may lead the conversation and loop in Support or RevOps [8].

**4. Amount.** Review the customer's usage and take the average of the past three months as the baseline [9]. Subtract the baseline from the spike to get the overage. Then use the pricing calculator to price the baseline volume and the baseline plus overage volume. The difference between the two prices is the refund amount [10]. Don't enter the overage alone into the calculator, because of tiered pricing [11]. Add a note to the Zendesk ticket with the calculation breakdown [12].

**5. Credit or refund.** Issue credits if the customer's period hasn't ended and the invoice isn't finalized [13]. If the invoice is finalized and this is a first request, issue a refund via a credit note [14].

**6. Issuing.** Refunds start in Billing Admin and are finalized in Stripe via a credit note [15]. You allocate the refund amounts per product manually [16].

**7. Escalate to RevOps** if something seems off, the customer has asked for multiple refunds lately, or the case doesn't match the simple cases [17]. Also escalate for big customers spending $1,667+ monthly [18], or if an invoice needs creating or changing [19].

You need to be switched to inactive in two places, and the handbook has a calibration step so you don't get flooded when you return.

**Stopping leads**
- In Salesforce, uncheck Is Active in the lead assignment tracker. [1]
- In Default (app → routing → queues), toggle your status to Inactive in each queue you're in. [2]
- Marking yourself "Out of Office" in your Default personal settings isn't enough. Someone still has to toggle you off in the queues manually. [3]

**Timing**
Two weeks is more than 5 days. You should be turned off 2 days before your time off starts, and turned back on the day you return. [4]

**Flooding when you're back**
The calibration step prevents it. While you're inactive, others in the queue keep getting leads, so their totals rise. Before you're reactivated, add the difference to your Calibration column in Default. For example, if others got +10 each, add +10. [5] Do the same with the Manual Leads Adjustment column in the Salesforce Lead Assignment Tracker. [6]

The excerpts don't say who does these steps for you, so check that with your team.

Yes, offer a trial, provided the prospect fits the criteria. A ~$40K deal is above the $20K sales-assist threshold. You should also have clear decision makers and a timeline, and the customer should want technical validation and be ready to invest time in an evaluation [1][2]. Skip the trial if there's no clear timeline or decision process, they're only price shopping, or they've already committed to buying [3].

Length: make it 2 weeks. The default is 2 weeks for $20-60K ARR unless there's a compelling reason for 4 weeks [4]. Go to 4 weeks only if the deal is over $60K ARR, the technical environment is complex, multiple stakeholders must validate, or they're comparing PostHog with other products [5].

If they ask for more time: extensions are common and fine, and the handbook says to be amenable [6]. For an extension of 7-30 days, ask for something in return, such as introductions to key stakeholders, a commitment to start procurement in parallel, verbal confirmation they're moving forward, or weekly check-ins until trial end [7]. Also find out why they need more time and what specifically has to be accomplished [8].

The handbook says every trial needs the SDK installed and events firing, documented success criteria, and a documented timeline [9].

answer:
You have two offers, depending on whether they're signing a prepaid deal.

1. **Prepaid deal with free credits.** For startup-plan customers who sign a prepaid deal, we offer two months of free credit [1]. They can claim it until the first billing date after their credits expire, even if they've used up their credits before then [1]. To present it:
 - Take their average monthly cost and multiply by 12 to estimate the prepaid amount [2].
 - Tell them they can buy credits for about 12 months of usage and get about 2 months of extra usage free, applied before the contract start date [2].
 - If they want to buy fewer credits, they get an extra 1/6 of the amount they buy, for free [2].
 - These free credits are one-time only [3]. Either apply them before the contract term, which means moving the contract start date 2 months later, or include them in the 12-month credit amount [3].

2. **Automatic transition bonus.** Once credits are used up or expired, teams move to a standard paid plan automatically. We email them and offer a one-time $500 credit bonus to soften the transition [4].

Credit extensions are not the norm. We don't usually extend credits, but exceptional cases can be requested [5]. Founders must explain why they couldn't use the credit in time and show evidence of recent progress. Customer Success reviews these requests manually [5].

answer:
Set up a trial in the billing admin (billing.posthog.com). Because they already have a paid subscription, you also need some extra steps so they aren't billed during the trial.

Prerequisites: the customer needs an Organization on EU or US Cloud, and you need billing admin access [1].

Create the trial:
1. Log in to Billing, open Trials in the sidebar, and click Add Trial [2].
2. Fill out the form. Set Status to Active, Target to what's needed (paid, teams, enterprise), and Type to Standard. Set the expiration to what's needed, such as 2 weeks, or 4 weeks for larger ($100k+) customers [2].
3. Click Save. After the trial date passes, their features reset to the free plan unless they've subscribed [2].

Extra steps for existing paid customers:
- Ask Mine to update Stripe and billing admin so revenue numbers aren't affected and the customer isn't billed during the trial [3].
- Remove the Stripe Subscription ID in Billing Admin, but keep the Stripe Customer ID [3].
- Set all products in the product map to a free status [3].
- Cancel the subscription in Stripe [3].
- Create a new subscription before the trial ends and update Billing Admin, so the move back to a paid plan doesn't disrupt the customer [3].

Trial length: the sales docs default to 2 weeks (for $20–60K ARR deals) and use 4 weeks for deals over $60K ARR [4]. Those lengths are written for new-business deals, so check they fit an existing customer's cross-sell.

The excerpts don't say whether an existing paying customer's cross-sell trial needs any other approval.

Customer comms are led by a Comms Lead, usually a PMM, who owns large-scale communication to users. But the Comms Lead doesn't update the status page or message VIP customers.

- **Comms Lead:** PMMs generally take responsibility for broad customer communication [1]. The Comms Lead takes ownership of any large-scale communication to users [2]. Marketing appoints one when external comms are needed [3].
- **Status page:** The Comms Lead is typically not responsible for updating it. That falls to the Incident Lead [4]. The Comms Lead only checks that it is accurate and current [5]. The support watcher can also help by making sure the messaging is clear, and can update it using /inc sp if needed [6].
- **VIP customers:** The Comms Lead doesn't handle these. Updating them is usually best handled by the Sales team [4]. In practice, account owners (AM/AE/CSM) send comms to their accounts using drafts from the Communications Manager On-Call (CMOC) [7].

Yes. For a new product, the best practice is at least one customer story within 3 weeks of launch [1]. Here is how to find a customer, based on the case study process:

1. Find the customer. Ask the PM for that product, because PMs do lots of user interviews and can suggest warm leads. You can also post in company Slack channels, with context on what you're looking for [2].
2. Make contact. Search for the company in Vitally first. If an Account Executive or CSM is assigned, give them a heads-up. If nobody is assigned, you can reach out directly. If the customer has a dedicated Slack channel, use that. Otherwise send an email [2].
3. Lay the groundwork. Once someone agrees to chat, make a GitHub issue to draft questions, tag the relevant sales/CS people, and note if you'll need artwork later [2].

What makes a good story: it should show that PostHog helped them achieve meaningful results and that they represent who we build for. It doesn't matter whether they pay us, use every tool, or have a big brand [2].

Case studies live in /contents/customers/ and appear on posthog.com/customers [2].
